task1.title: Class sizes in primary schools in four Australian states (2010)
task1.prompt: The pie charts show the size of classes in primary schools in four states in Australia in 2010.

chartDesc.xAxis: Australian states and territories (New South Wales, South Australia, Australia Capital Territory, Western Australia)
chartDesc.overview: Classes of 30 students or more accounted for the smallest proportion across all four areas, ranging from 4% to 7%. Conversely, classes with 26–30 students made up the largest share in three out of the four regions, peaking at 51% in the Australia Capital Territory.
keyFeatures: Classes of 30 students or more were the smallest category in every state/territory: 4% in NSW and South Australia, 5% in Western Australia, and 7% in ACT.
The 26–30 students category was the largest in ACT (51%), Western Australia (42%), and NSW (37%).
In South Australia, 20 students or fewer formed the largest category at 35%, compared to 33% for 26–30 students.
The 21–35 students group ranged from a high of 33% in NSW to a low of 10% in ACT.

task1.instruction: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
task1.sampleBand8:
The four pie charts compare the distribution of class sizes in primary schools in four Australian states — New South Wales, South Australia, the Australia Capital Territory and Western Australia — in 2010.

Overall, classes of 26–30 students made up the largest single group in most states, while the biggest classes, those of 30 students or more, were rare everywhere, never exceeding 7% of the total.

In the Australia Capital Territory, just over half of all classes (51%) contained 26–30 students, the highest figure recorded anywhere, and a further 38% had 20 students or fewer, so smaller classes clearly dominated there. Western Australia showed a similar, though less extreme, pattern, with the same two categories accounting for 42% and 26% respectively.

By contrast, class sizes were more evenly spread in the other two states. In New South Wales, 37% of classes had 26–30 students and a further 33% fell into the 21–35 group, while in South Australia classes of 20 students or fewer were actually the most common, at 35%. In every state the 30-or-more category was the smallest of all, ranging from just 4% in New South Wales and South Australia to 7% in the capital territory.

To'rtta doiraviy diagramma 2010-yilda Avstraliyaning to'rt shtatidagi — Yangi Janubiy Uels, Janubiy Avstraliya, Avstraliya Poytaxt Hududi va G'arbiy Avstraliyadagi — boshlang'ich maktablarda sinf o'quvchilari sonining taqsimotini solishtiradi.

Umuman olganda, ko'pchilik shtatlarda 26–30 o'quvchili sinflar eng katta yagona guruhni tashkil etdi, eng katta — 30 va undan ortiq o'quvchili — sinflar esa hamma joyda kam uchrab, jami ulushi hech qachon 7 foizdan oshmadi.

Avstraliya Poytaxt Hududida barcha sinflarning yarmidan sal ko'prog'i (51%) 26–30 o'quvchidan iborat bo'ldi — bu qayd etilgan eng yuqori ko'rsatkich — yana 38 foizida esa 20 yoki undan kam o'quvchi bor edi, demak u yerda kichikroq sinflar yaqqol ustunlik qildi. G'arbiy Avstraliyada ham shunga o'xshash, ammo uncha keskin bo'lmagan manzara kuzatildi: xuddi shu ikki toifa mos ravishda 42 va 26 foizni tashkil etdi.

Bundan farqli o'laroq, qolgan ikki shtatda sinf hajmlari ancha tekis taqsimlangan edi. Yangi Janubiy Uelsda sinflarning 37 foizi 26–30 o'quvchili bo'lib, yana 33 foizi 21–35 toifasiga to'g'ri keldi, Janubiy Avstraliyada esa 20 yoki undan kam o'quvchili sinflar 35 foiz bilan aslida eng keng tarqalgani bo'ldi. Har bir shtatda 30 va undan ortiq toifasi eng kichigi bo'lib, Yangi Janubiy Uels va Janubiy Avstraliyadagi atigi 4 foizdan poytaxt hududidagi 7 foizgacha oraliqda o'zgardi.

task2.title: Local history versus world history
task2.prompt: It is more important for schoolchildren to learn about local history than world history. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
task2.instruction: Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
task2.sampleBand8:
History teaching in schools often has to strike a balance between the story of the local area and that of the wider world. Although I fully accept the value of local history, I disagree with the idea that it deserves priority, because in my view the two complement each other and are equally important.

Learning about local history undoubtedly brings real benefits. It gives children a strong sense of identity and civic pride, and because the past is visible in nearby buildings, museums and monuments, it feels tangible rather than abstract. A pupil who understands how their own town developed is often more motivated to study the subject as a whole, since the material connects directly to their daily surroundings.

However, concentrating on local events at the expense of world history would leave students with a dangerously narrow perspective. Today's children grow up in a deeply interconnected world, and they cannot make sense of migration, trade, climate negotiations or international conflicts without understanding the global forces that shaped them. Studying other societies also develops critical thinking and empathy, as it forces students to see events from perspectives very different from their own — skills that purely local content cannot provide.

In conclusion, while local history is a valuable and motivating part of the school curriculum, I do not believe schools should prioritise it over world history. The most effective approach is to use the local past as a gateway into the global story, so that schoolchildren understand both where they come from and the wider world they belong to.
task2.uzSampleBand8:
Maktablarda tarix o'qitish ko'pincha mahalliy hudud tarixi bilan kengroq dunyo tarixi o'rtasida muvozanat topishni talab qiladi. Mahalliy tarixning qadrini to'liq tan olsam-da, unga ustuvorlik berish kerak degan fikrga qo'shilmayman, chunki nazarimda bu ikkisi bir-birini to'ldiradi va bir xil darajada muhimdir.

Mahalliy tarixni o'rganish, shubhasiz, chinakam foyda keltiradi. U bolalarda kuchli o'zlik tuyg'usini va fuqarolik g'ururini shakllantiradi, o'tmish esa yaqin-atrofdagi binolar, muzeylar va yodgorliklarda ko'zga ko'rinib turgani uchun mavhum emas, balki qo'l bilan tutsa bo'ladigan narsadek tuyuladi. O'z shahri qanday rivojlanganini tushungan o'quvchi ko'pincha fanni umuman o'rganishga ko'proq qiziqadi, chunki material uning kundalik muhiti bilan bevosita bog'lanadi.

Biroq dunyo tarixi hisobiga faqat mahalliy voqealarga e'tibor qaratish o'quvchilarda xavfli darajada tor dunyoqarash qoldirgan bo'lardi. Bugungi bolalar chuqur o'zaro bog'langan dunyoda ulg'aymoqda va ularni shakllantirgan global kuchlarni tushunmasdan turib migratsiya, savdo, iqlim muzokaralari yoki xalqaro nizolarning mohiyatini anglay olmaydi. Boshqa jamiyatlarni o'rganish, shuningdek, tanqidiy fikrlash va hamdardlikni rivojlantiradi, chunki u o'quvchilarni voqealarga o'zinikidan butunlay farq qiladigan nuqtai nazarlardan qarashga majbur qiladi — bu ko'nikmalarni faqat mahalliy mazmun bera olmaydi.

Xulosa qilib aytganda, mahalliy tarix maktab o'quv dasturining qimmatli va qiziqish uyg'otadigan qismi bo'lsa-da, maktablar uni dunyo tarixidan ustun qo'yishi kerak deb hisoblamayman. Eng samarali yondashuv — mahalliy o'tmishdan global tarixga ochiladigan darvoza sifatida foydalanish, shunda maktab o'quvchilari ham o'z ildizlarini, ham o'zlari mansub bo'lgan kengroq dunyoni tushunadilar.
